Study on synergistic effect of carrier combined with micro-aeration on 
anaerobic digestion of food waste

A B S T R A C T
Enhancing the conversion efficiency of methane production from food waste (FW) is always a hot issue. Bio­
logical carriers and micro-aeration had demonstrated notable advantages in enhancing anaerobic digestion (AD) 
efficiency, but their synergistic potential remained largely untapped. This study introduced polyurethane carriers 
into micro-aeration assisted AD, trying to explore their synergism in enhancing the digestive efficiency of FW. 
Results revealed that an optimal blend of carriers and micro-aeration pose significant improvement to the 
digestive performance. Their combination enhanced microbial metabolic activity, accelerated the consumption 
or conversion of dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecules, promoted the aggregation of microorganisms, which 
improved their tolerance capacity under the oxygen stress brought by the micro-aeration, ensuring the system 
stability. It also enriched methane-producing microorganisms, and balanced methane-producing pathways. 
Additionally, the combination of micro-aeration and carriers promoted key enzyme expression in metabolic 
pathways, providing ample support for methane production. These findings held significance for optimizing FW 
treatment, improving methane production efficiency, and reducing the burden of organic waste treatment.
1. Introduction
In recent years, the management of organic waste, particularly food 
waste (FW), has become a global significant environmental challenge. It 
is predicted that 2.5 billion tonnes of FW are going to be generated by 
2025 annually worldwide [1]. FW not only poses a threat to public 
health but also contributes to the emission of greenhouse gases, leading 
to climate change. Among the various available treatment methods, 
anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as a promising technology for 
efficiently converting FW into renewable energy and valuable by- 
products, with the process terminated by methanogenesis [2]. Howev­
er, the problem of low organic matter conversion efficiency during AD 
has been consistently limiting its practical application [3,4]. Therefore, 
improving the conversion efficiency of FW organics into methane is a 
crucial concern.
Several studies have explored ways to improve the performance of 
AD, such as substrate pre-treatments [1], optimizing process parameters 
[5] and introducing additives [6]. However, the pretreatment or 
supplementary additives usually required extra energy and chemicals, 
which not only increased operational costs and complexity but also gave 
rise to a range of environmental issues. Recent studies have shown that 
micro-aeration, which involves injecting small amounts of air or oxygen 
(typically ranging from 0.005 to 5 L O2/LR-d) into an anaerobic system, 
with cost-effectiveness, has gained attention as a potential strategy for 
improving digestive performance due to its ability to accelerate the 
hydrolytic-acidification process, which provides more available sub­
strate for methanogenesis [7,8]. Compared to strict anaerobic condi­
tions, injecting trace amount of air creates a higher oxidation–reduction 
potential (ORP) environment that reshapes the microbial community in 
the digester. Facultative anaerobes involved in the hydrolytic- 
acidification process are stimulated and exhibit much higher activities. 
An appropriate micro-aeration contributes to the enhancement of the 
hydrolysis-acidification process and thus facilitates subsequent meth­
anogenesis [9]. Ruan et al. [10] found that micro-aeration can enhance 
the microbial activity, increase substrate degradation rates, and improve 
overall process stability. Furthermore, according to Fu et al.’s research

in digestion of corn stover, micro-aeration contributed to promote the 
biodiversity of facultative hydrolytic bacteria and acidifying bacteria 
[11]. Although the advantages of micro-aeration have been reported, 
precise control of oxygen dose is required when applying micro-aeration 
to substrates with high hydrolysis rates. Excessive aeration beyond the 
oxygen consumption and anti-oxidation capacities of facultative bacte­
ria may have detrimental effects on obligate anaerobes, as high con­
centrations of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) can damage their 
phospholipid membranes and DNA [12].
Another key factor contributing to the poor performance of AD is the 
limited energy acquisition rate of anaerobic microorganisms, resulting 
in slow growth, particularly for methanogenic archaea [13,14]. In the 
AD of organic matters, daily slurry discharge poses a risk of expelling 
slow-growing microorganisms from the reactor, leading to an insuffi­
cient population of functional microorganisms. So, introduction of mi­
crobial attachment media is helpful for retaining functional anaerobes 
through formation of microbial agglomerations or biofilms [15]. Under 
the effect of the attachment media, here coexist of the attached biofilm 
and suspended sludge in the digester, which not only improves the 
number of microorganisms, but also effectively retains the slow-growing 
functional anaerobes involving in anaerobic conversion of organic pol­
lutants [16]. Though some small particles such as zeolite, active carbon 
(AC), magnetite and et al, have been utilized in current researches, they 
pose insufficient surface for microorganism attach [17–19]. Besides the 
porous structures, biocompatibility is an important index for the media 
[20], which determines the efficiency of mass transfer between sub­
strates and microbes [21]. Polyurethane is a synthetic polymer hydro­
philic bio-carrier with interconnected pores, has multiple advantages 
because of its important properties like adsorption, bio-attachment, high 
porosity and contains some cationic surface active groups and hydro­
philic groups such as hydroxyl, which enable firm fixation of microbes 
and enzymes onto the surface [22]. Wang et al.[23] discovered that the 
application of polyurethane carriers in digesters for municipal biowaste 
(FW, fruit-vegetable waste and dewatered sewage sludge) improved the 
digestive efficiency, and enhanced the microbial retention. It also 
contributed to high system stability due to the reduced mass-transport 
resistance and high microbe density of the biofilm. Shi et al.[24] have 
proved that adding polyurethane carriers to reactors increases microbial 
richness and diversity, benefiting their long-term stability. Additionally, 
the filling ratio of the attachment media also poses some impacts. A low 
filling ratio may result in poor substrate flow, while a high filling ratio 
can affect substrate diffusion and metabolites [25].
Considering the effectiveness of both bio-carriers and micro-aeration 
in enhancing AD, their combination may demonstrate even greater po­
tential. Biofilms can mitigate the toxic effects of micro-aeration on 
obligate anaerobes [26,27]. Additionally, biofilms can effectively trap 
slow-growing functional microorganisms (e.g., methanogenic archaea), 
while facultative bacteria with higher energy metabolism through aer­
obic respiration can grow in suspension, utilizing enhanced biological 
activity to improve their ability to hydrolyze and acidify organic matters 
[24,28]. Complex organic compounds are hydrolyzed into dissolved 
organic matter (DOM) during the hydrolysis and acidification stage, and 
DOM is further fermented into volatile fatty acids (VFA) [29], providing 
metabolizable substrates for slow-growing archaea attached to the sur­
face of the carrier, thereby enhancing overall treatment efficiency. DOM 
serves as the primary substrate for VFA production by fermentation 
bacteria. Many studies have shown that the characteristics and varia­
tions of DOM significantly impact the final utilization of DOM products, 
with changes in VFA and biogas production closely linked to variations 
in DOM characteristics [30–32]. However, it is currently unclear 
whether carrier and micro-aeration affects the characteristics of sludge 
DOM molecular composition, and how the key DOM components are 
transformed and utilized in methanogenesis. Traditional spectroscopic 
analysis methods can only characterize the DOM composition at a macro 
level, making it difficult to reveal the DOM composition features and 
their relationship with AD at the molecular level. Fourier transform ion 
cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS), with its ultra-high 
resolution (>200,000), mass accuracy (error < 0.000001), and sensi­
tivity, can completely separate complex organic molecular mass spec­
trometry peaks in DOM, thus enabling the resolution of DOM 
composition features at the molecular level [33].
The above analysis has shown that both bio-carriers and micro- 
aeration can effectively promote AD. However, research on their com­
bined application in this process remains limited, particularly within 
solid waste treatment. Therefore, this paper tries to combine bio-carriers 
and micro-aeration to enhance AD performance of FW. The study first 
analyzed the operational performance of the reactor to evaluate their 
promotion effects and obtain the optimal operating conditions. Then, 
carrier morphology, enzyme activity, and DOM characteristics under 
these conditions were compared. Finally, metagenomic sequencing was 
used to explore the reactor’s metabolic pathways, revealing underlying 
microbial regulatory mechanisms. The results of this study provide new 
insights for further enhancing the digestive performance of FW.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Digester configuration and operational conditions
The anaerobic digester was made of a plexiglass cylinder (inner 
diameter 8 cm, height 25 cm) with an effective working volume of 0.7 L, 
including a feed hopper, a mixing shaft, a separate jacketed thermostat 
and gas collection device (Fig. S1). The polyurethane foam carriers were 
purchased from Henan Tianyi Environmental Protection Technology 
Co., Ltd. Detailed information can be found in Table S1, and the actual 
photo is also presented in the supporting information (Fig. S2). Experi­
ments were conducted with different filling ratios (V carrier/V reactor) of 0 
% (D0), 10 % (D10), 20 % (D20), and 30 % (D30). The AD systems were 
operated in semi-continuous feeding mode to maintain a constant hy­
draulic retention time (HRT) of 20 d, with an organic loading rate (OLR) 
of 2.5 g VS/L‧d, and the digestion temperature was maintained at 35 ± 1 
℃ by a thermostat water bath (HH-501, Xinbao, China). At the end of 
each discharging-feeding, the reactors were flushed with N2 gas for 5 
min to remove the air.
Anaerobic inoculum was obtained from Tangjiatuo Wastewater 
Treatment Plant located in Chongqing, China. The inoculum was settled 
naturally under anaerobic conditions for 1 day to remove the superna­
tant, and then the resulting sludge was filtered through a 20-mesh sieve 
to remove large impurities. The prepared inoculum was stored at 
anaerobic conditions of 35 ± 1 ℃ for more than a week before use to 
eliminate the interference of residual biodegradable organic matter to 
subsequent AD process. The substrate FW was artificially prepared in the 
laboratory following the formula stated in [34]. The details of FW and 
inoculum are listed in Table 1. The digester was run continuously for a 
total of 85 days and was divided into two stages according to whether 
micro-aeration was introduced, namely the without micro-aeration 
stage (day 1–35) and the micro-aeration stage (day 36–80). During the 
second stage, a uniform and gradual introduction of air was achieved by

injecting 5 mL using a syringe after each feeding, resulting in an increase

2.2. Chemical and physical analysis
pH was determined by pH meter (FE28, METTLER TOLEDO, 
Switzerland). Measurements of total solid (TS), volatile solid (VS) and 
chemical oxygen demand (COD) were conducted in accordance with 
standard methods [35]. Carbohydrates, crude protein and crude fat 
were quantified according to [36]. The biogas composition and volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs) were determined by a gas chromatography (GC1690, 
Jiedao, Hangzhou). The operation process of gas chromatography was 
introduced in detail in our previous study [37]. The extraction method 
of EPS refers to the study of [38]. The PN and PS of each form of EPS 
were determined as the total amount by Lowry-Folin method and phe­
nol–sulfuric acid method, respectively [39]. α-Glucosidase activity, ATP 
content, acetate kinase, ATP and coenzyme F420 were measured by using 
the ELISA kit (Shanghai hengyuan biological technology co., LTD). The 
morphology of the carrier and suspended sludge was observed using a 
fluorescence microscope (SEM, Hitachi S-4800, Leica, Germany). Spatial 
microstructure of suspended sludge was visualized by CLSM (Leica, TCS 
SP8 STED 3X, Germany). Detailed staining and observation were per­
formed according to the previously reported method by [40].
2.3. FT-ICR-MS analyses
Supernatants were separated from the samples of digested sludge by 
centrifuge at 6000 rpm for 20 min, and filtered through 0.45 μm 
membrane. The filtered supernatant was further diluted to TOC=2 ~ 3 
mg/L with an ultrapure water to avoid protein precipitation in DOM 
[41]. Solid phase extraction (SPE) was performed using PPL cartridges 
(BondElute PPL, 6 mL, 500 mg, Agilent Technologies, USA) after 
determination of DOC in the supernatants. The molecular composition 
of DOM was characterized using Bruker SolariX FT-ICR-MS (15.0 T 
superconducting magnet) equipped with electrospray ionization (ESI) 
ion source. Samples for ESI FT-ICR-MS analysis were continuously 
infused into the ESI unit by syringe infusion at a flow rate of 120 μL/h. 
The ESI needle voltage was set to −
4.0 kV, and the ion accumulation 
time was set to 0.2 s, mass range of 100–1600 Da. A total of 300 
continuous 4 M data FT-ICR transients were added to enhance the 
signal-to-noise ratio and the dynamic range. The range of m/z was set 
from 100 to 800. A sodium formate solution (10 mM) was used to 
externally calibrate the instrument, and the known series of natural 
organic matter (NOM) was used to internally recalibrate the spectra. The 
detailed operation is described in the Supporting Information.
2.4. Metagenomic sequencing and analysis
The anaerobic biomass samples were collected the reactors at the end 
of Stage II and III and stored in −80 ◦C for microbial analysis. The DNA 
extraction of the samples was performed using the E.Z.N.A.® Soil DNA 
Kit (Omega Bio-tek, USA). After the extraction of genomic DNA, the 
concentration and purity of DNA were detected using TBS-380 and 
NanoDrop2000 respectively, and the integrity of DNA was determined 
by 1 % agarose gel electrophoresis. Fragmentation of DNA was achieved 
using Covaris M220 (Gene Company, China) to obtain fragments of 
approximately 400 bp. The PE library was constructed using the 
NEXTFLEX Rapid DNA-Seq kit (Bioo Scientific, USA). The bridge PCR 
amplification was followed by sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq/ 
Hiseq Xten platform (Illumina, USA) for metagenomic sequencing.
The raw data was quality-controlled using the Fastp software. The 
reads were aligned to the host DNA sequences using the BWA software, 
and contaminant reads with high similarity were removed. The opti­
mized sequences were assembled using the MEGAHIT software based on 
the principle of succinct de Bruijn graphs. Contigs with a length of ≥
300 bp were selected from the assembly results as the final assembly. 
The contigs were then subjected to ORF prediction using MetaGene, and 
the gene sequences predicted from all samples were clustered using the 
CD-HIT software to construct a non-redundant gene set. Finally, the 
SOAPaligner software was used to align the high-quality reads of each 
sample to the non-redundant gene set (with 95 % identity) and to 
calculate the abundance of genes in the corresponding samples.
2.5. Statistical analysis
The experimental data underwent analysis of variance (ANOVA) for 
statistical processing. All physicochemical index data presented in this 
paper are expressed as “mean ± standard deviation” (n = 3) to improve 
clarity. Student’s t test was utilized to determine whether significant 
differences existed between different systems, with a p-value below 0.05 
considered statistically significant. Statistical mapping was conducted 
using Origin 9.0 software.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Digestive performance
Fig. 1 shows the digestive performance of different digesters. It was 
obvious that the presence of carriers increased methane production 
(Stage I). The averaged specific methane yield for D20, D30, and D10 are 
390.7, 381.6, and 350.6 mL CH4/g⋅VS, which are much higher than that 
of D0 (about 330.1 mL CH4/g⋅VS). The specific methane production in 
the D30 reactor is lower than that in D20, possibly due to the excessive 
input of carrier, affecting the liquid-phase mass transfer in the digester.

Previous studies have pointed out that a high filling rate of carriers can 
lead to an increase in biofilm thickness, affecting the supply of substrates 
and the discharge of metabolites within the internal biological phase, 
thereby increasing mass transfer resistance [42].
After introducing micro-aeration in stage II, the methane production 
for all digesters got increased, indicating that the micro-aeration has a 
positive effect on methane production. As can be seen from the figure, 
the micro-aeration treatment resulted in a slight improvement in 
methane production in the control group (D0), with a specific methane 
yield of 368.84 mL CH4/g⋅VS. Zhou et al.’s study also indicated that the 
promoting effect of low-dose oxygen on methane production in AD was 
not significant [43]. With the proceeding of the micro-aeration, there is 
a rapid increase in VFA concentration in D0, resulted in declining in the 
methane yield. However, when carrier was present in the digester, the 
introduction of micro-aeration gained more promotion of the methane 
production, particularly for D20 (417.7 mL CH4/g⋅VS), reaching 1.13 
times that of the control. Compared the system failure at the end of the 
experiment in the control digester, the participation of the carrier 
ensured the stability of the digester without declining of the methane 
production.
As important intermediate compounds in methane production 
metabolism, VFAs’ concentration is a crucial consideration for the 
optimal performance of biogas digesters. Therefore, it is necessary to 
monitor VFA concentrations to study the stability and efficiency of 
biogas digesters. Fig. 2b depicts the TVFAs’ concentration throughout 
the experiment. In stage I, the TVFAs concentration in the carrier groups 
remained relatively stable. In contrast, the TVFAs concentration in the 
control group (D0) fluctuated greatly. The polyurethane carrier pro­
vided attachment and growth space for microbial cells, reducing the risk 
of microbial loss and increasing the stability of the anaerobic digestion 
system [23]. As the reactor operated and entered the early period of 
stage II, the control group (D0) exhibited relatively stable TVFA con­
centrations and pH values. However, with the continuous introduction 
of micro-aeration, the TVFAs’ concentration increased gradually to as 
high as 800 mg/L, while the pH value slowly declined to around 7.1, 
indicating the occurrence of acidification within the system. This may be 
attributed to the generation of ROS during the reaction process, which 
could have exerted a certain toxic effect on obligate anaerobes such as 
methanogenic archaea [44]. Compared to the control digester (D0), the 
TVFA in the carrier participated groups maintained at much lower 
concentration levels, ensuring the stable pH throughout the experiment. 
It is also noticed from the figure that there was a slight accumulation of 
TVFA in D30 and D20 during the early stage after micro-aeration 
introducing. This can be ascribed that the archaea were still in the 
adaptation period to the new environment, posing lower acids con­
sumption rate to the acid generation in the hydrolytic-acidification 
process [45]. The microbial community gradually adapts to the micro- 
aerobic environment, and thus the system maintained stable 
throughout the experimental period [46].
3.2. Microbial metabolic activity
Considering the highest methane production efficiency observed in 
D20, it was selected for in-depth analysis in the subsequent study. AD is 
a biological process catalyzed by microorganisms through the secretion 
of specific enzymes, and the enzymes activities reflects the metabolic 
activities of microorganisms. Therefore, enzyme activities in different 
digesters were monitored and compared (Fig. 2). α-glucosidase is the 
main extracellular hydrolytic enzyme in anaerobic metabolism [47]. 
Without micro-aeration, the activity of α-glucosidase in D20 is 128 % of 
that in the control group (D0), verifying the positive effect of the carrier. 
Further enhancement of α-glucosidase activity was observed in D0 and 
D20 when micro-aeration was introduced into the digester. Similar to 
α-glucosidase, micro-aeration also led to an increase in the activity of 
acetate kinase (ACK), especially in the digester containing the carrier. 
The increased activities of α-glucosidase and ACK verified that the 
micro-aeration enhanced the hydrolytic-acidification process [34]. The 
carrier provided a habitat for functional bacteria responsible for hy­
drolysis and acidification, promoting better interactions among bacte­
ria, enzymes, and substrates to facilitate the conversation of organic 
matters [48]. In addition, the ATP content in the system also exhibited a 
significant increase during the stage II, approximately a 37 % and 18 % 
rise in ATP levels for D0 and D20. Previous studies have demonstrated 
that the addition of trace oxygen as a terminal electron acceptor in 
anaerobic bioreactors can accelerate the hydrolysis of complex organic 
compounds by facultative bacteria and enhance the electron transfer 
activity in microbial metabolism [49]. The reduction of O2 by NADH 
(Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) releases a substantial amount of 
energy, leading to the generation of a proton gradient that drives ATP 
synthesis and the transport of other metabolites, thereby increasing the 
overall system’s productivity and metabolic efficiency [50].
Methane production during AD determines heavily by the activities 
of methanogenic archaea. The presence of coenzyme F420, acting as a 
distinct electron carrier, can reflect the activity of methanogenic archaea 
[51]. As shown in Fig. 2, the coenzyme F420 content in digesters D0 and 
D20 in stage I was 35.07 and 36.98 IU/L. After the introduction of micro- 
aeration, the activity of F420 increased in both digesters. These findings 
indicated that micro-aeration can enhance the secretion of F420 by mi­
croorganisms [3]. Furthermore, in the digesters with carriers, the co­
enzyme F420 content was higher than in the control. This reveals that the 
micro-oxygen environment conducive to archaea’s metabolic activity 
[47], by potentially inducing their aggregation to form biofilm on the 
carrier to cope with oxygen stress [52].
3.3. EPS content and spatial distribution of biopolymers
Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) secreted by microorgan­
isms were a main component in biofilms, which can embed microbial 
cells in a three-dimensional matrix within the floc, playing an important 
role in maintaining the stability of the sludge floc and protecting mi­
crobial cells [30,53]. In Fig. 3a, EPS were classified as loosely bound (L- 
EPS) and tightly bound (T-EPS) ones based on their degree of combi­
nation to the cell surface, with their composition characterized by pro­
tein and polysaccharide concentrations. In the absence of micro- 
aeration, higher levels of various EPS were observed in the carrier 
group compared to the control group. This observation confirms that the 
carrier created a favorable environment for microbial proliferation and 
attachment, thereby promoting microbial growth and EPS production. 
After micro-aeration was implemented, a significant increase was 
observed in both the L-EPS and T-EPS of the control group. Surprisingly,

the distribution of different EPS components in the D20 digester un­
derwent substantial changes. The L-EPS content decreased while the T- 
EPS content showed a steep increase, surpassing that of L-EPS by a large 
margin. T-EPS possesses a distinct shape and forms a tight, stable 
attachment to the cell surface, contributing to the improved stability of 
the system during micro-aeration operation [54]. In terms of composi­
tion, it was evident that PN constituted a high proportion, while the 
content of PS was minimal and almost negligible. Earlier research had 
indicated that hydrophobic proteins in EPS facilitated microbial aggre­
gation and promoted biofilm formation [55]. This effect could be 
attributed to the abundance of negatively charged amino acids in pro­
teins, making them more prone to electrostatic binding with multivalent 
cations-a crucial factor in stabilizing aggregate structures [56].
To further visualize the attachment behavior of key microorganisms 
during the micro-aeration stage, SEM analysis was conducted on the 
sludge in D0 and the carrier in D20, to reveal their differences in mi­
crobial morphology. The surface of the sludge appeared coarse with 
dispersed microbial distribution in D0 (Fig. 3b). In contrast, the micro­
organisms in D20 carriers exhibited a denser structure, with plump and 
clearly distinguishable microbial cells. A layer of biofilm was deposited 
on the surface of microorganisms, with rod-shaped and spherical mi­
croorganisms distributed and embedded within it (Fig. 3c). Ultimately, 
anaerobic microorganisms were almost enveloped by the macromolec­
ular metabolites to protect them from the toxicity of ROS. Moreover, the 
spatial distribution of organic biopolymers (including nucleic acids 
(red), α-D-glucopyranose polysaccharides (yellow), proteins (green), 
and β-D-glucopyranose polysaccharides (blue)) in the sludge after 
micro-aeration treatment was observed using CLSM. SYTO 63, Con A- 
AF555, FITC, and calcofluor white fluorescent substances were respec­
tively used for labeling, with Merged representing the combined images 
of the four dyes. The staining results revealed that the sludge was 
surrounded by PN and PS, which were considered as the primary con­
tributors to biofilm formation [57]. Proteins and β-D-glucopyranose 
polysaccharides were primarily concentrated within the core of aggre­
gates, while nucleic acids and α-D-glucopyranose polysaccharides were 
positioned at the periphery (Fig. 3d and 3e). This distribution pattern 
suggested a possible correlation with EPS, consistent with the findings of 
regarding EPS and cell distribution in granules [40]. The network 
structure of PS molecules promoted sludge flocculation, with β-PS as the 
backbone of the network playing a significant role. α-PS, PN, lipids, and 
cells easily associated with β-PS to maintain the structural stability of 
flocs and improve sludge bio-flocculation accordingly [58]. Notably, the 
D20 sample exhibited heightened protein secretion by cells, with a 
significant presence of filamentous microorganisms and a denser cell 
distribution, tending to aggregate into clusters (Fig. 4e). After micro- 
aeration, the increase in protein content of EPS in digester D20 
enhanced the physical bridging of neighboring bacterial cells and 
formed a cross-linked network by binding with polyvalent cations and 
organic molecules [59] (Fig. 3a). This phenomenon might be linked to 
microorganisms creating a denser EPS structure for self-preservation 
during stressful environmental conditions.
3.4. DOM molecular characteristics
3.4.1. General characteristics of sludge DOM
Dissolved organic matter (DOM) are believed to be a carbon source 
that microorganisms can directly assimilate during AD [60]. Under­
standing the transformation of organic components in AD can be greatly 
facilitated by identifying the characteristics of DOM. In this study, FT- 
ICR-MS was used to identify 4571,5859,4808 and 3397 molecules in 
D0-I, D20-I, D0-II and D20-II, respectively, with detailed molecular 
characteristics summarized in Table 2. The molecular weight

distribution of the compounds was monitored between 100–800 m/z, 
with relatively abundant compounds distributed in the range of 
300–500 m/z, accounting for around 55 % of the total (Fig. S3a). The 
double bond equivalents (DBE) represent the total number of double 
bonds and rings in a molecule, and can be used to characterize degree of 
unsaturation or complexity of the molecule. A higher DBE value signifies 
a wider variety of compounds with an increased number of double bonds 
and rings. The nominal oxidation state of carbon (NOSC) is related to the 
biogeochemical reactivity and bioavailability of organic compounds, 
with organic molecules possessing high NOSC values being more ther­
modynamically favorable for degradation [61,62]. In the initial stage, 
DOM in D20 exhibited higher DBE and NOSC values (Fig. S3), poten­
tially attributable to the addition of the carrier resulted in higher reac­
tivity in biogeochemical reactions. Conversely, the DOM in D0 exhibited 
relatively lower values, indicating the presence of recalcitrant stable 
compounds that were difficult to be degraded [62].
Analysis of the molecular weight distribution (Fig. 4a) and changes 
in aromaticity equivalent (Fig. 4b) reveals that D20 exhibited a lower 
molecular range and decreased aromaticity after micro-aeration treat­
ment, corresponding to its lower Mw and AIw values. Both DBE and 
NOSC in D20 were shifted towards lower values (Fig. S3). Kellerman 
et al.[63] showed that intrinsic molecular properties were crucial for the 
overall reactivity of organic matter. Specifically, degradation processes 
preferentially removed DOM characterized by highly oxidized states and 
aromatic compounds, while reduced and aliphatic compounds exhibited 
resistance to degradation or underwent tight cycling. Consequently, the 
primary constituents in D20 were reduced (low NOSC) and aliphatic

Additionally, it was found that the DOM molecules in D20 exhibited 
lower O/Cw and DBEw, while DOM molecules in D0 showed the opposite 
trend, indicating that large DOM molecules in D20 sludge are tend to be 
hydrolyzed into smaller organic molecules with higher saturation, lower 
oxygen content, and fewer aromatic structures under the effect of micro- 
aeration. Studies have shown that such organic compounds typically 
represent more biodegradable components readily be utilized by mi­
croorganisms during AD [60]. Although DBE has been widely used to 
characterize complex samples, its drawback is that compounds with 
heteroatoms (e.g., O, S) can overlap in terms of DBE. For instance, ox­
ygen and sulfur don’t affect the DBE value, but they may add to the 
potential double bonds [64]. Therefore, to estimate the number of C–C 
double bonds in AD mixtures, (DBE-O)/C was utilized to further visu­
alize the changes in DOM induced by carriers and micro-aeration. Based 
on the positive and negative values of (DBE-O)/C and NOSC, the sludge 
DOM molecules were classified into four categories (Table S2). A higher 
positive value of (DBE-O)/C indicated increased unsaturation, while a 
higher positive NOSC value signified greater oxidation [65]. The FW 
DOM molecules were predominantly in a reduced state, with more un­
saturated species than saturated species, and fewer molecules in the 
oxidized state region (Fig. 4d), indicating that unsaturated and reduced 
compounds were preferentially decomposed by the enhancement of 
micro-aeration [66,67].
3.4.2. Composition and transformation of DOM
The above analysis revealed significant differences in the general 
characteristics of DOM molecules in D0 and D20 before and after micro- 
aeration treatment, prompting further investigation into whether micro- 
aeration affected the molecular composition of DOM in the digested 
organics. By utilizing the different H/C and O/C characteristics of 
typical compounds, the Van Krevelen diagram of DOM molecules was 
divided into seven categories of typical compounds, demonstrating the 
distribution of compounds and differences in molecular composition 
among DOM samples [68] (Fig. S4). Based on the elemental composition 
of DOM molecules, the DOM molecules in sludge were classified into 
four types (CHO, CHON, CHOS, and CHONS). Among them, CHO and 
CHON compounds were the predominant constituents of DOMs in 
sludge, with CHON compounds representing the highest proportion, 
ranging from 36.21 %~44.04 % of the total DOM molecules (Table 2). 
This suggested that the released DOM molecules mainly comprised

of certain organic compounds (e.g. cysteine, serine, sulfur-containing 
amino acids), although difficult to be degraded in AD themselves, can 
promote the degradation of VFAs by decreasing oxidation–reduction 
potential, mediating electron transfer, and enhancing microbial meta­

In Fig. 5a, lignins were observed to be the predominant compound 
type in all digesters. The proportion of lipid compounds in group D0 was 
significantly higher than in D20, indicating the poor biodegradability of 
lipids pre-existing in FW or/and generated through microbial activities 
in D0 [73]. Compared to the control group, adding bio-carriers increased 
unstable compound abundance (e.g., proteins, carbohydrates and un­
saturated hydrocarbons). After micro-aeration introduction, lipid and 
protein compounds in the control group significantly decreased, indi­
cating that the micro-aeration promoted the degradation of lipid and 
protein substances, which were key precursors for bacteria to produce 
VFAs [74]. Protein and unsaturated hydrocarbon levels decreased in 
D20, while lignin and condensed aromatic levels increased. Continuous 
degradation of proteins and unsaturated hydrocarbons enriched aro­
matic structures during AD. Studies have shown that the decomposition 
of protein macromolecules induced by hydroxyl groups contributes to 
the enrichment of condensed aromatic compounds in sludge EPS [75]. 
Lignin-derived compounds are a typical type of recalcitrant DOM, con­
taining reducible groups such as alkoxy or hydroxy substituents conju­
gated to aromatic rings via ether-linkages [33]. The increase in lignin- 
derived DOM may be due to the degradation of carboxylic and alicy­
clic compounds, which were components of many microbial cell enve­
lopes and natural metabolites [76].
In addition, visualization was conducted for the shared and unique 
molecules in D0 and D20 to further elucidate the transformation of DOM 
molecules before and after the micro-aeration treatment (Fig. 5b and 
5c). In stage I, there were 2203 shared DOM molecules in D0 and D20, 
primarily concentrated in the region of H/C>1.0. Following micro- 
aeration treatment, the distribution range of DOM molecules shared 
by D0 and D20 did not change significantly, but the number of these 
shared molecules decreased. The unique DOM molecules in D0 
increased, indicating that micro-aeration promoted the release or gen­
eration of organic matter in D0. In contrast, the unique DOM molecules 
in D20 significantly decreased, possibly due to enhanced microbial ac­
tivity in D20 after micro-aeration, accelerating the consumption or 
transformation of DOM molecules.
3.5. Microbial community structure
The process of turning large molecules into methane relied on 
cooperation among different microbial communities. Therefore, study­
ing the changes in microbial species composition is helpful for under­
standing the inner mechanism. From the bacterial community 
composition of D0 and D20 sludge samples at the genus level, despite 
similarities in bacterial composition between them, their relative 
abundances varied (Fig. S5a). Bacteroidota, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, 
and Chloroflexi were dominant phyla in each sample. Among them, 
Bacteroidota and Firmicutes were two typical hydrolytic-acidification 
bacteria, playing a significant role in the hydrolysis of organic matter 
and acidogenesis during AD. Bacteroidota was reported to have the 
ability to hydrolyze polysaccharides and proteins [77], while Firmicutes 
could secrete extracellular enzymes closely related to the metabolism of 
proteins and lipids [78]. During micro-aeration assisted AD, the relative 
abundances of Bacteroidota and Firmicutes in digester D0 both increased. 
Firmicutes were also associated with the conversion of polysaccharides to 
butyric acid, propionic acid, and acetic acid [79], possessing thick cell 
walls and the ability to produce endospores to survive under extreme 
conditions [80]. The higher relative abundance of Bacteroidota and Fir­
micutes in D0 after micro-aeration indicated their strong ability to 
degrade complex substrates, thus leading to a higher hydrolysis rate. In 
contrast to the control group, the changes in Bacteroidota in digester D20 
were opposite to Firmicutes. Bacteroidota and Firmicutes had similar 
growth conditions (substrates, optimum temperature, and pH value), so 
they might have competed with each other for the degradation of 
polysaccharides and proteins in the digester. The abundance of Actino­
bacteria, which was associated with humus formation and organic 
matter degradation, decreased with the introduction of micro-aeration 
[81]. The introduction of micro-aeration might have had a certain 
inhibitory effect on Actinobacteria, showing its poorer oxygen-tolerance. 
Chloroflexi, reported to be one of the important glucose-degrading mi­
crobial communities responsible for acid production and H2 oxidation 
homoacetogenesis in the AD process [82], could utilize various carbo­
hydrates and amino acids as substrates [78]. The increase in their 
relative abundance in the carrier added group confirmed the increase in 
α-glucosidase activity under micro-aerobic conditions (Fig. 2), which 
could enhance the hydrolysis of polysaccharides and other complex 
organic substrates. Additionally, significant enrichment of Tenericutes 
and Candidatus_Cloacimonetes was found in digester D20 compared to 
D0, indicating that the utilization of carrier and micro-aeration enriched 
the microbial community structure, enhanced the utilization and 
transformation of organic matters, which ensured the system stability in 
D20 group.
At the genus level, notable disparities existed in the archaeal com­
munity structure between the carrier and control groups (Fig. S5b). The 
dominant archaea in the control and carrier groups were Methanothrix 
and Methanosarcina. Methanothrix is an obligate acetatoclastic metha­
nogen, while Methanosarcina is a mixotrophic methanogen that can 
utilize acetate or H2 and CO2 as substrates for methane production [83]. 
Before and after micro-aeration, Methanothrix remained relatively stable 
in the control group, indicating that Methanothrix had certain adapt­
ability to oxygen. In the presence of trace amount of oxygen, H2 tends be 
oxidized by aerobic respiration to ensure the thermodynamic feasibility 
of syntrophic fatty acid oxidation [43], which insures the conversion of 
VFAs to acetate. This explained why Methanothrix has a relatively high 
abundance with less acetate accumulation. After introducing micro- 
aeration, the relative abundance of Methanosarcina in the D20 system 
decreased by 27.40 %. The decrease in Methanosarcina was accompanied 
by the enrichment of Methanothrix, with its relative abundance 
increasing from 1.58 % to 11.99 %. Methanoculleus is an obligate 
hydrogenotrophic methanogen that can use H2/CO2 and formate as 
carbon sources to produce CH4. It was enriched in the D20 system after 
micro-aeration, suggesting that micro-aeration was beneficial to the 
growth of Methanoculleus. Methanobacterium is another methanogen 
utilizing H2 present in all samples but with a relatively low abundance of 
approximately 1.50 % at D0. Following micro-aeration treatment, the 
abundance of Methanobacterium further decreased, indicating that 
micro-aeration inhibited its growth [84]. Compared to D0, the relative 
abundance of Methanobacterium increased at D20 after micro-aeration, 
which may be a result of the carrier alleviating the toxic effects of ox­
ygen. Overall, compared to the control group, a good balance of two 
methane production pathways was achieved at D20.

3.6. Changes in key metabolic pathways
Above microbial analysis revealed that carriers and micro-aeration 
posed significantly influence on the microbial communities with 
distinct functions in the digestive system. To gain deeper insights into 
the impact of carriers, micro-aeration, and their combination on mi­
crobial metabolic functions and to explore the enhancement mechanism 
of methane production, the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes 
(KEGG) database was used to annotate metabolic pathways before and 
after micro-aeration treatment (Fig. S6, Table S3). The results show that 
the relative abundance of oxidative phosphorylation, pyruvate meta­
bolism, butyrate metabolism, and methane metabolism pathways were 
found to be significantly up-regulated under the effect of micro-aeration. 
Considering the key roles of specific functional enzymes in metabolism, 
enzymes expressions in these pathways were analyzed to understand the 
function mechanism of the micro-aeration with or without carriers.
3.6.1. Oxidative phosphorylation
It is well known that oxidative phosphorylation is one of the basic 
pathways for ATP biosynthesis. Through micro-aeration treatment, 
pathways related to oxidative phosphorylation in D0 and D20 showed 
significant enhancement, with higher relative abundances of carrier 
groups compared to the control group (Fig. S6, Table S4). This suggested 
that micro-aeration enhanced ATP biosynthesis, crucial for cellular 
metabolism and various biochemical reactions requiring energy. As 
illustrated in Fig. 6a, oxidative phosphorylation synthesis of ATP is 
composed of a series of embedded membrane enzyme complexes as 
electron carriers. Notably, except for complex III, the other four parts got 
improved after micro-aeration treatment (Fig. 6b). Complexes I, III, and 
IV facilitated the transfer of protons from the matrix to the outer side of 
the inner membrane, generating a proton concentration gradient 
essential for driving ATP synthesis and electron transfer to subsequent 
electron transporter. After micro-aeration treatment, the relative 
abundances of NADH dehydrogenase nuoEFHJ and nuoCD in complex I 
in the carrier added digester were significantly higher than those in the 
control group, catalyzing the oxidation of NADH, transferring electrons 
to coenzyme Q, and pumping H+ out of the inner membrane. Complex II 
also posed a significant increase in the relative abundances of sdhABCD 
and frdABCD, which promoted the oxidation of succinic acid. Complex 
III: the cytochrome c reductase complex UQCRFS1, facilitated the 
transfer of electrons from CoQ to cytochrome c and simultaneously 
pumped protons out of the inner membrane, contributing to the proton 
gradient. Complex IV is a cytochrome c oxidase complex, the relative 
abundances of COX15 and coxB got markedly improved after micro- 
aeration, catalyzing the reduction of O2 to form H2O and releasing H+
in the intermembrane space. Complex V: a pivotal step in ATP synthesis, 
showed increased relative abundances of the key functional genes after 
micro-aeration, including ATP synthases (ATPF1ABEDG, ATPF0ABC, 
ppa, ppaX, ppk1, and ppk2), indicating the enhancement in ATP syn­
thesis (Fig. 6b). The increase in ATP production could enhance the

3.6.2. Vfas metabolism
All life activities are energy consuming reactions, and a high level of 
energy supply may contribute to the conversion of organic matter and 
the generation of methane. The metabolism of pyruvate is the main 
pathway for VFA transformation, with acetic acid as the final product. 
The expression of this metabolic process and related genes is shown in 
Fig. 6c. Glucose was initially broken down into phosphoenolpyruvate. 
Pyk is essential in glycolysis and encodes a pyruvate kinase. After micro- 
aerobic introduction, the expression of pyk in the carrier group was 
upregulated, 1.5 times higher than in the control group. This upregu­
lation of pyk facilitated the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate into 
pyruvate, providing more substrate for pyruvate metabolism to generate 
acetic acid. As shown in Fig. 6c, pyruvate was converted into acetic acid 
and acetyl-CoA, and the relative abundance of enzymes involved in the 
pyruvate metabolism pathway showed a significant upward trend after 
micro-aeration treatment. The relative abundance of the aceE gene, 
encoding pyruvate dehydrogenase, was higher in the carrier added 
group than the control group, and further increased after introduction of 
micro-aeration, possibly promoting the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl- 
CoA. DLAT is the functional gene of dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase, 
which accepted the acetyl group formed by the oxidative decarboxyl­
ation of pyruvate and transferred it to CoA. aceE and DLAT cooperated 
to convert pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, participating in subsequent 
methane metabolism. Por and Kor are pyruvate ferredoxin oxidore­
ductases, which directly converted pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. AckA is a 
phosphotransferase, and its increased abundance enhanced the yield of 
acetate. In butyric acid metabolism, genes such as ato, ptb, buk, and 
ACSM were significantly upregulated in the carrier group after micro- 
aeration, indicating that the combination of carrier with micro- 
aeration enhanced the conversion of butyric acid to acetyl-CoA. phbB 
and paaH were genes encoding acetyl-CoA acyltransferases, whose 
relative abundance in the carrier group and control group significantly 
increased by the micro-aeration, 1.4 times and 2.1 times higher than the 
micro-aeration absent stage (Table S5). ACAT is an acetyl-CoA acyl­
transferase, whose abundance was also significantly increased by the 
micro-aeration, far exceeding that of the control group.
In addition to the above pathways, the relative abundance of fatty 
acid metabolism, methane metabolism and ABC transporter proteins 
were improved by the micro-aeration. ABC transporter proteins are 
present on the cell membrane and transport substances inside and 
outside the cell membrane through synergistic action with ATPase [85]. 
ABC transporter proteins have numerous substrates, involving nutrients 
and signal transduction molecules represented by vitamins, amino acids 
and metal ions [86]. Changes in the ABC transporter reflect substrate 
utilization. The abundance of methane metabolism increased by 9.24 % 
and 5.13 %, and the abundance of fatty acid metabolism increased by 
6.89 % and 6.45 % in the D20 group and D0 group. The enhancement of 
fatty acid metabolism may facilitate the hydrolysis of fatty into VFAs 
and provide available substances for the subsequent methane meta­
bolism. Methane metabolism is a crucial process in methane production, 
the D20 group showed a significant increase in the abundance of genes 
encoding key enzymes compared to D0, especially pta, mtr, and mcr. 
Among them, pta is one of the important enzymes for methane pro­
duction from acetate metabolism, while mtr and mcr are related to the 
synthesis of methyl coenzyme A and the reduction of methyl coenzyme. 
The significant upregulation of these genes after micro-aeration indi­
cated the strengthening of methane production pathways in the D20 
group, thereby promoting methane production. Furthermore, the 
abundance of ABC transporter proteins in both groups increased after 
micro-aeration. After micro-aeration treatment, the relative abundance 
of ABC transporter proteins increased by 7.53 % and 11.23 % in the D20 
and D0 groups, respectively (Table S3). The upregulation of ABC 
transporter protein abundance indicates an improved utilization rate of 
nutrients in the digestive system.
The metabolic state of organisms during the digestion process is also 
closely associated with DOM. The complex composition of DOM mole­
cules contains valuable molecular information regarding the metabolic 
state, including reaction substrates, metabolic transformation products, 
and microbial metabolic by-products [87]. During the AD hydrolysis and 
acidification stage, complex organic matter undergoes hydrolysis into 
DOM and subsequent fermentation into VFAs. Notably, pyruvate, 
butyrate, and acetate metabolism play a crucial role in the acidification 
of DOM substrates, as evidenced by the significant upregulation of key 
genes involved in these metabolic pathways following micro-aeration 
treatment. This upregulation suggests that acidogenic bacteria can 
more efficiently utilize DOM substrates, leading to the formation of in­
termediates that promote increased methane production. Moreover, the 
carrier group demonstrated enhanced metabolic functions after the 
micro-aeration treatment, which could be attributed to the heightened 
utilization of DOM and consequently explained its highest methane 
production.
4. Conclusions
This study aimed to promote the digestive efficiency of FW through 
combining biological carriers with micro-aeration, and to elucidate the 
transformation of DOM molecules and the regulation mechanism of 
microorganisms. The results indicated that an appropriate combination 
of carriers (filling rate of 20 %) with micro-aeration improved the 
methane yield from 390.7 mL CH4/g VS in Stage I to 417.7 mL CH4/g VS, 
which was 1.13 times higher than the control group (368.84 mL CH4/ 
g⋅VS). The synergistic effect of micro-aeration and carriers ensured 
digester stability, created a favorable microenvironment, enhanced 
microbial metabolic activity, expedited the consumption or conversion 
of DOM molecules, resulting in a reduction of unique DOM molecules in 
D20 by 59.71 %. Additionally, this approach facilitated EPS secretion, 
accelerated biofilm formation on the carriers, and provided protection 
for methanogens against oxygen stress. Moreover, the combination of 
micro-aeration and carriers enriched the structure of the microbial 
community, promoted the expression of key enzymes in metabolic 
pathways such as acetate metabolism, butyrate metabolism, and 
oxidative phosphorylation, providing sufficient substrate and energy 
support for the subsequent methane production metabolism.
